newsitem.title: USA: U.S. "furious" over Serb boycott of Bosnia chamber.
newsitem.headline: U.S. "furious" over Serb boycott of Bosnia chamber.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it was "furious" over the Bosnian Serbs' boycott of the first session of Bosnia's peacetime parliament, and threatened new sanctions unless they complied with the Dayton peace accords.

Foreign dignitaries, including U.S. envoy John Kornblum, waited for more than three hours on Saturday for Serb representatives to appear at the ceremony in Sarajevo, but they failed to show up, claiming security concerns.
"The United States government was furious with the decision by (Serb leader Momcilo) Krajisnik not to participate," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns.
"It was an important, symbolic event which was meant to kick off a new era in Bosnia."
Burns said officials from the U.S. embassy in Sarajevo met Krajisnik on Sunday and delivered a "very stiff letter" from Kornblum, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European and Canadian Affairs.

"This letter put Krajisnik and his colleagues on notice that we expect them to take steps rapidly -- in the next couple of days -- to demonstrate their commitment ... to the peace process, to the Dayton accords," he told reporters.

Last November's Dayton pact created a single Bosnian state divided into a Moslem-Croat federation and a Serb republic. But Serbs have continued to proclaim their goal of creating their own state and merging with Serbia.

The United States says that, following Bosnia's first post-war elections on Sept. 14, it is urgent to set up joint institutions including a presidency, parliament, council of ministers, central bank and supreme court.

Burns said that following a further contact earlier on Monday with Krajisnik, who represents the Serbs on the three-man Bosnian presidency, the United States was "expecting better behaviour" from the Serbs.
Kornblum had also told Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic to exert pressure on the Bosnian Serbs to make them comply with Dayton, he added.

Burns said U.S. officials had highlighted to the Bosnian Serbs that when the U.N. Security Council last week lifted sanctions against them, and against Serbia, it reserved the right to reimpose them if there was no compliance.

"The United States will not hesitate to bring this issue up in the U.N. Security Council should we come to believe over the next weeks that the Bosnian Serbs are fundamentally unwilling to meet their commitments," he said.
Burns said the United States would give the Serbs "some time to right the wrongs" but said large amounts of economic aid were ultimately at stake.
"If the Bosnian Serbs keep this up, all that aid's going to go in the other direction," he said, presumably referring to the Moslems and Croats.

He said Kornblum, who returned to Washington on Sunday night, would go to Europe for a meeting in London on Thursday of the Contact Group on Bosnia. The United States, Britain, France, Germany and Russia are members of the group.

"One of the major issues on the agenda will be this sorry performance by the Bosnian Serbs, and by Thursday, we hope that they'll have taken some specific steps to reverse themselves on this," he said.
